About

I am a chemist with research interests in semiconductor nanomaterials, photocatalysis, inorganic materials and analytical characterisation.

My work combines experimental materials research with chemical and spectroscopic techniques to investigate the composition, structure and properties of materials. It includes the synthesis of ZnS nanoparticles and ZnS–TiO₂ nanocomposites for photocatalytic studies, and the multi-analytical characterisation of Harappan pottery.

I also worked as a Research Chemist intern at the Central Archaeological Laboratory, Lahore Fort, where I took part in the cleaning, analysis, documentation and conservation of archaeological objects. Alongside this, I teach chemistry at college level.

I am looking for a research-based master's programme where I can connect materials chemistry, photocatalysis and advanced characterisation. Water splitting and heterostructure design are directions I want to learn, not work I have already done.

Project 1 · MSc thesis

Synthesis and Characterization of ZnS–TiO₂ Nanocomposites for Photocatalytic Applications

Zinc sulphide nanoparticles were synthesised, combined with TiO₂, characterised by UV-Vis, FTIR and SEM, and tested for photocatalytic degradation of an organic dye under natural sunlight. Supervisor: Dr Waseeq Ahmad Siddiqui, University of Sargodha.

  • ZnS + TiO₂
  • UV-Vis
  • FTIR
  • SEM
  • Photocatalysis

WorkflowSynthesis, characterisation, testing

  1. ZnSZinc acetate with TBAC capping agent, H₂S bubbled through
  2. TiO₂ solTTIP in ethanol and nitric acid, 70 °C
  3. Composites1, 3, 5, 7 and 10 % TiO₂ added during ZnS formation
  4. CharacteriseUV-Vis, FTIR and SEM
  5. TestMurexide dye, 100 minutes in sunlight

ResultsSpectra and images

Switch between pure ZnS and the 5 % ZnS/TiO₂ composite. Click any figure to enlarge it. Samples are my own thesis work, prepared as listed above.

Key finding

Under the tested conditions (murexide 5 mM, natural sunlight, 100 minutes), neither pure ZnS nor the 5 % ZnS/TiO₂ composite showed measurable dye degradation.

Interpretation and limitations

The wide-band-gap materials absorb mainly in the UV, so limited UV in natural sunlight may be one contributing factor. This was not measured, and I do not treat it as the established cause. Without a dye-only control, a dark-adsorption step and a calibrated light source, the result cannot be explained further. XRD and TEM were not available to confirm composite formation, so I make no heterostructure claim.

Next steps
  • Controlled UV and visible light source, with a dye-only control and dark adsorption
  • Test the other TiO₂ ratios already prepared (1, 3, 7 and 10 %)
  • XRD for phase identification, Tauc plots for band gap, and electron microscopy if available

Project 2 · Archaeometry

Multi-Analytical Characterization of Harappan Pottery

Three pottery sherds from Harappa, excavated in 1926 and kept in the Harappa Museum, Sahiwal, were examined by five complementary methods to describe their composition, mineral phases and surfaces.

  • 3 sherds
  • XRF + PXRF
  • XRD
  • FTIR
  • SEM-EDX
CompositionRich in silica and alumina: SiO₂ 56–60 %, Al₂O₃ about 19 %, Fe₂O₃ 6.6–7.2 %.
MineralsXRD shows quartz and feldspar together with clay minerals.
OrganicsWeak aliphatic C–H bands in FTIR could indicate organic residues.
SurfacesSEM shows sintered surfaces and cracks. Fibre-like features may be plant temper.

SamplesThe sherds (HPS-1, 2, 3)

Sherds as received, then cut into small pieces for SEM and ground to powder for XRF, XRD and FTIR. Click a photo to enlarge it.

ElementsWhat the instruments found

Nineteen elements showed up across XRF, portable XRF and EDX. Select an element to see which method detected it.

Alkali and alkaline earthMetals and siliconNon-metalsRare earths

XRFBulk composition

Fig. 5. Benchtop XRF of powdered sherds HPS-1, HPS-2 and HPS-3, major oxides in wt %. The three samples are close in silica, alumina and iron. Calcium is the oxide that moves most.

HPS-1HPS-2HPS-3wt %

Calcium oxide rises from 1.3 % to 4.1 % across the three sherds, so the clay is not identical in every sherd.

XRDMinerals

Fig. 6. XRD of powdered sherds. All three diffractograms are dominated by one strong peak near 27° 2θ, the main quartz reflection. Select a peak on the schematic to read it.

Schematic illustration, not measured data: redrawn from the measured peak positions, with approximate heights and simulated baseline noise. The measured patterns are on the right.

FTIRFunctional groups

Fig. 7. FTIR of powdered sherds. Bands indicate what is bound in the clay and whether organic material may remain. Select a band on the wavenumber axis.

Schematic band map: positions are as measured on HPS-1, HPS-2 and HPS-3, heights are illustrative. The axis runs from high to low wavenumber.

SEM-EDXSurfaces

Fig. 8. SEM-EDX of cut sherd pieces. Micrographs show sintered surfaces with cracks and pores. Fibre-like features in the cross-sections may be plant temper, which I have not confirmed.

Interpretation and limitations

Three sherds allow a comparison of composition and mineral phases. They do not support any claim about clay source, firing temperature or provenance.

  • Next steps: more sherds and reference clays
  • Petrography of thin sections
  • Thermal analysis (TGA/DTA)
  • Trace-element analysis for provenance
